sagrada-familia:
A family chosen by God

The Holy Family is the name the Church gives to the family of Jesus, Mary and Joseph. It all begins in Nazareth, when the angel Gabriel announces to Mary, a young woman betrothed to Joseph, that she would become the mother of the Son of God by the power of the Holy Spirit. Mary answers in faith: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord." Joseph, a just man, planned to send her away quietly so as not to expose her, but an angel explains the mystery to him in a dream, and he takes Mary as his wife.

Bethlehem, Egypt and Nazareth

Because of a census ordered by the emperor, the couple travels to Bethlehem, the town of David. There, with no room at the inn, Jesus is born and laid in a manger. Shepherds and later the Magi from the East come to adore him. When King Herod decides to kill the boys of Bethlehem, Joseph is warned in a dream and flees with Mary and the Child to Egypt. Once the danger has passed, the family returns and settles in Nazareth, in Galilee.

The Gospel also tells of the presentation of Jesus in the Temple, where the aged Simeon and the prophetess Anna recognize him as the Savior, and of the time when Jesus, at twelve years old, stayed behind in Jerusalem talking with the teachers of the Law while Mary and Joseph searched anxiously for him for three days.

The hidden life

After that, the Gospel sums up thirty years in a single sentence: Jesus was obedient to his parents and grew in wisdom, stature and grace. These were years of work in Joseph's carpentry shop, of family prayer and of simple life in a small village. Christian tradition holds that Joseph died before Jesus began his public life, with Jesus and Mary at his side.

A model for every family

Devotion to the Holy Family grew greatly from the seventeenth century on. Pope Leo XIII encouraged it, and in 1921 Benedict XV extended its feast to the whole Church. Today it is celebrated on the Sunday after Christmas. The Church presents Jesus, Mary and Joseph as a model of faithful love, shared faith, honest work and trust in God in times of trouble, reminding us that every family can be a small "domestic Church."
miguel:
"Who is like God?"

Saint Michael is one of the three archangels called by name in Sacred Scripture. His name in Hebrew is a question: "Who is like God?" It is at the same time an act of humility and a battle cry against the pride of the one who wanted to put himself in the Creator's place.

Michael in the Bible

In the book of the prophet Daniel, Michael appears as "one of the chief princes," the great protector of God's people who will arise in the time of final distress. In the letter of Saint Jude he disputes with the devil over the body of Moses and says only: "May the Lord rebuke you!" And in the Book of Revelation he leads the faithful angels in the battle in heaven against the dragon, "the ancient serpent," who is defeated and cast down. That is why Christian art shows him in armor, with a sword or spear, overcoming the devil beneath his feet.

A devotion across the centuries

Christians have called upon him since the earliest centuries. At the end of the fifth century, tradition tells of his apparitions on Mount Gargano in southern Italy, where one of the oldest shrines dedicated to him arose. In 708, on the coast of France, Bishop Aubert built in his honor what would become the famous Mont-Saint-Michel. It is also said that during a plague in Rome, Pope Gregory the Great saw an angel sheathing his sword above Hadrian's mausoleum, a sign that the epidemic was over; the place came to be called Castel Sant'Angelo.

Protector in the fight against evil

In 1886 Pope Leo XIII ordered a prayer to Saint Michael to be said at the end of Mass, asking for his defense "in battle" against "the wickedness and snares of the devil." This prayer is still widely prayed today, and Pope John Paul II urged the faithful not to forget it. The feast of Saint Michael is celebrated on September 29, together with Gabriel and Raphael. He is the patron of police officers, soldiers and all who protect others, and he is also remembered as the one who accompanies souls at the hour of death.
gabriel:
The strength of God

The name Gabriel means "strength of God" or "God is my strength." He is the archangel of great messages: in Scripture, whenever he appears, he brings news that changes history. That is why he is called God's messenger above all others.

The visions of Daniel

The first time the Bible calls him by name is in the book of Daniel. While the prophet was trying to understand mysterious visions about empires and future times, Gabriel comes "in swift flight," at the hour of the evening offering, to give him understanding and explain the meaning of what he had seen, including the famous prophecy of the seventy weeks, which Christians read as announcing the coming of the Messiah.

Zechariah and Mary

Centuries later, in the Temple in Jerusalem, Gabriel appears to the priest Zechariah beside the altar of incense and announces that his wife Elizabeth, elderly and barren, would bear a son, John, who would prepare the way of the Lord. Zechariah doubts and is struck mute until the child is born. Six months later, Gabriel is sent to Nazareth, to a virgin named Mary, and greets her: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you!" He announces that she would conceive by the Holy Spirit the Son of the Most High, whom she would name Jesus. When Mary asks how this can be, he answers that "nothing is impossible for God." That greeting became the beginning of the Hail Mary, the prayer Christians repeat more than any other.

Patron of those who communicate

Because he carried the most important news in history, the Incarnation of the Son of God, Gabriel was proclaimed by Pope Pius XII in 1951 patron of telecommunications. He is invoked by postal workers, journalists, broadcasters, diplomats and all who work carrying messages. His feast is celebrated on September 29, together with Michael and Raphael, and the Church remembers him in a special way every time it prays the Angelus, which recalls the moment of the Annunciation.
rafael:
"God heals"

Raphael is the third archangel called by name in the Bible, and his name means "God heals." His whole story is in the Book of Tobit, a tender narrative about God's providence in the life of a faithful family in hard times.

A family in trial

Tobit was an Israelite exiled in Nineveh, a just man who gave alms and buried the dead of his people, even at the risk of his life. One day he went blind and, discouraged, asked God to let him die. At that very hour, in another city, a young woman named Sarah was also praying in anguish: she had been given in marriage seven times, and every husband had died on the wedding night because of a demon. God heard both prayers and sent Raphael to help them.

The traveling companion

Tobit sent his son, young Tobiah, to collect money he had left in safekeeping in a distant land. A young man who said his name was Azariah offered to go with him: it was Raphael in disguise. On the way, beside the Tigris River, a fish attacks Tobiah, and the angel teaches him to catch it and keep its gall, heart and liver. When they reach Sarah's house, Raphael advises Tobiah to ask for her hand; through prayer and the remedy from the fish the demon is driven away, and the two are married. On the way home, Tobiah rubs the gall on his father's eyes, and Tobit sees again.

Only then does the companion reveal who he is: "I am Raphael, one of the seven angels who stand ever ready before the glory of the Lord." He explains that he presented that family's prayers and good works to God, and asks them to give thanks and praise God.

Patron of travelers and caregivers

Because of this story, Raphael is invoked as protector of travelers, of doctors, nurses and pharmacists, of the blind and of all who seek healing in body or soul. He is also remembered by young people asking God for a good marriage. His feast is September 29, together with Michael and Gabriel.
agostinho:
A restless heart

Augustine was born in 354 in Thagaste, in North Africa, in what is now Algeria. His father, Patricius, was a pagan; his mother, Monica, a Christian of deep faith. Very gifted, he studied rhetoric in Carthage and lived a turbulent youth there: he lived with a woman without marrying her, had a son with her, Adeodatus, and for about nine years followed Manichaeism, a sect that promised to explain good and evil. At nineteen, reading a book by Cicero awakened in him a passion for wisdom that never left him.

From Carthage to Milan

A teacher of rhetoric, he moved to Rome and then to Milan. Monica followed him, praying and weeping for his conversion. In Milan, Augustine went to hear the sermons of Bishop Ambrose out of curiosity, to study his eloquence, and ended up moved by what he said. In 386, in anguish in a garden, he heard a child's voice repeating "take and read." He opened Saint Paul's letter to the Romans and read the call to leave a disordered life and put on Christ. "All the shadows of doubt were dispelled," he later wrote. At the Easter Vigil of 387 he was baptized by Ambrose together with his son. Soon afterward Monica died at peace in Ostia.

Bishop of Hippo

Back in Africa he wanted to live as a monk with friends, but the people of Hippo asked for him as a priest in 391, and a few years later he was made bishop. For more than thirty years he preached, cared for the poor, judged the people's disputes and defended the faith against the divisions of the Donatists and against the Pelagians, who downplayed the need for God's grace. He wrote the "Confessions," in which he tells his life as one long prayer, and "The City of God," after the sack of Rome in 410.

The Doctor of Grace

Augustine died on August 28, 430, while the Vandals were besieging Hippo. He is one of the greatest Doctors of the Church, called the "Doctor of Grace," and his most famous line sums up his story: "You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you."
tomas-aquino:
A young man who stood up to his family

Thomas was born around 1225 in the castle of Roccasecca, near Aquino in Italy, into a noble family. At five he was taken to the Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, and his family dreamed that one day he would be abbot of that powerful monastery. While studying in Naples, however, he met the Dominicans, poor friars who lived on alms and devoted themselves to preaching, and he decided to join the order. His brothers kidnapped him on the road and kept him confined at home for about a year. It is said that they even sent a woman to tempt him, and that he drove her out with a burning brand from the fire. Nothing made him give up.

The "dumb ox"

Once free, he went to study under Saint Albert the Great in Paris and Cologne. Big, quiet and humble, he was nicknamed the "dumb ox" by his classmates. Albert, who knew his worth, replied that one day the bellowing of that ox would be heard throughout the world. Thomas became a professor at the University of Paris and in several cities in Italy, uniting faith and reason like no one else: he showed that philosophy, including that of Aristotle, could help us understand revealed truth more deeply.

The Summa Theologiae

He wrote dozens of works, among them the "Summa contra Gentiles" and the "Summa Theologiae," still today the foundation of the study of Catholic theology. At the request of Pope Urban IV he composed the texts for the feast of Corpus Christi, with hymns such as the "Pange Lingua," whose last verses form the "Tantum Ergo," still sung before the Blessed Sacrament. He prayed before studying and said he had learned more before the crucifix than from books.

"All that I have written seems like straw"

In December 1273, after a profound experience during Mass, he stopped writing, saying that everything he had written seemed like straw compared with what he had seen. He died on March 7, 1274, at the abbey of Fossanova, on his way to the Council of Lyon. He was canonized in 1323 and declared a Doctor of the Church, the "Angelic Doctor." He is the patron of students and of Catholic schools and universities.
teresa-avila:
A girl who wanted heaven

Teresa de Cepeda y Ahumada was born in Ávila, Spain, on March 28, 1515. As a child she read the lives of the saints with her brother Rodrigo, and the two ran away from home determined to die as martyrs in Moorish lands; an uncle found them on the road and brought them back. She lost her mother at thirteen and asked Our Lady to be her mother. As a teenager she loved tales of chivalry, fine clothes and conversation, but at twenty, against her father's wishes, she entered the Carmelite Monastery of the Incarnation in Ávila.

Years of struggle and a new conversion

Soon after her vows she fell gravely ill; she spent days unconscious and everyone thought she had died. She recovered slowly, but for almost twenty years, in her own words, she lived a life divided between God and worldly distractions, even abandoning prayer for a time. Around 1554, before an image of the deeply wounded Christ, she was profoundly moved and gave herself completely. Then began an intense life of prayer, with mystical graces she described with great simplicity.

Reformer of Carmel

Longing to live the Carmelite rule with more poverty, silence and prayer, in 1562 she founded the small convent of Saint Joseph in Ávila, the first of the Discalced Carmelites. She faced distrust, lawsuits and persecution, but, always with good humor and obedience, she founded seventeen convents of nuns in all, traveling across Spain in carts, often ill. With Saint John of the Cross she also brought the reform to the friars. She said God can be found even "among the pots and pans" and that prayer is "an intimate sharing between friends" with the One we know loves us.

Teacher of prayer

Out of obedience she wrote "The Book of Her Life," "The Way of Perfection" and "The Interior Castle," masterpieces of spirituality. She died in Alba de Tormes in October 1582, saying, "After all, I die a daughter of the Church." Canonized in 1622, she was the first woman declared a Doctor of the Church, by Paul VI in 1970. Her feast is October 15.
antonio-padua:
Fernando of Lisbon

Saint Anthony was born in Lisbon around 1195 and baptized with the name Fernando. As a young man he joined the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine, first in Lisbon and then at the monastery of Santa Cruz in Coimbra, where he spent years studying the Bible and the Fathers of the Church, acquiring an impressive memory and knowledge.

The Franciscan call

In 1220 the bodies of five Franciscan friars martyred in Morocco arrived in Coimbra. Moved by their witness, Fernando asked to enter the new order of Saint Francis, took the name Anthony and set out for Africa, longing also to give his life for Christ. There he fell gravely ill and, when he tried to return, a storm drove his ship to Sicily. In 1221 he took part in the great gathering of the friars in Assisi, where he saw Saint Francis, and was sent to a humble hermitage in Italy, where no one knew of his learning.

The preacher who drew crowds

At a priestly ordination in Forlì, no one had been prepared to preach, and he was asked to say a few words. Everyone was amazed at his wisdom and fervor. From then on he preached throughout Italy and southern France, confronting the Cathar heretics with the Word of God. Saint Francis authorized him to teach theology to the friars. Tradition says that in Rimini, when the heretics refused to listen to him, he went to the seashore and the fish came to hear his sermon. His crowds were so large that he had to preach outdoors.

A saint for the whole world

Worn out by his labors, he died near Padua on June 13, 1231, at about thirty-six years of age. He was canonized less than a year later, one of the fastest canonizations in history, and in 1946 he was declared a Doctor of the Church. He is invoked to find lost things, as protector of the poor, through "Saint Anthony's bread," and in Brazil and Portugal as a saint who helps people find a spouse. He is shown with the Child Jesus in his arms, recalling a vision he received.
francisco-sales:
A young nobleman and a crisis of faith

Francis de Sales was born on August 21, 1567, at the castle of Sales in Savoy, a region between France, Switzerland and Italy. His father wanted him to have a career as a lawyer and statesman. He studied in Paris with the Jesuits and then law at the University of Padua, where he earned his doctorate. While still in Paris he went through a terrible crisis: he became convinced he was damned and lived for weeks in anguish. He was set free while praying before an image of Our Lady, surrendering himself to God's love even without understanding everything. From that trial was born the serene trust that would mark his whole life.

Missionary of the Chablais

Against the wishes of his father, who had already arranged a marriage and a post for him, he became a priest in 1593. Soon afterward he volunteered to go to the Chablais, a region that had become Calvinist. For four years he faced cold, closed doors and even attempts on his life. Since hardly anyone would come to listen, he wrote leaflets explaining the Catholic faith and slipped them under the doors. Through patience, kindness and dialogue, most of the region returned to the Church. Because of those leaflets he was later proclaimed patron of journalists and writers.

Bishop and guide of souls

In 1602 he was named bishop of Geneva, but since the city was Calvinist he lived in Annecy. He preached, visited the mountain parishes, taught catechism to children and received everyone with a gentleness he won through great effort, for he had a strong temper. He used to say that "you catch more flies with a drop of honey than with a barrel of vinegar." With Saint Jane Frances de Chantal he founded the Order of the Visitation in 1610.

Holiness for everyone

His book "Introduction to the Devout Life" taught that holiness is not only for priests and religious but for the soldier, the merchant, the mother of a family, each in his or her own state of life. He also wrote the "Treatise on the Love of God." He died in Lyon on December 28, 1622. He was canonized in 1665 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1877. His feast is January 24.
catarina-sena:
The dyer's daughter

Catherine Benincasa was born in Siena, Italy, on March 25, 1347, one of the youngest of the many children of Giacomo, a cloth dyer, and Lapa. At six she had a vision of Christ above the church of Saint Dominic, and soon afterward she secretly promised to consecrate her life to God. When her family wanted her to marry, she cut off her hair and firmly resisted. Her parents finally accepted, and she began to live a life of prayer and penance at home, in a small room where she spent almost three years in silence.

Serving the sick and the condemned

Around the age of sixteen she joined the "Mantellate," laywomen of the Dominican Third Order who lived in their own homes. After a time of seclusion she felt Christ calling her to serve others: she cared for the sick, even the most repulsive cases, and during the plague of 1374 she tended the dying without fear of contagion. The story became famous of a young man condemned to death, Niccolò di Toldo, whom she accompanied to the scaffold, holding his head as he died in peace, reconciled with God.

A woman who spoke to popes

Though she had no formal education, she dictated letters to kings, rulers and popes, pleading for peace and the reform of the Church. In 1375 she received the stigmata, which remained invisible until her death. In 1376 she went to Avignon, in France, where the popes had lived for almost seventy years, and encouraged Gregory XI to return to Rome, which he did the following year. Later, during the Great Western Schism, she fought for the unity of the Church around Pope Urban VI. She also dictated the "Dialogue," a conversation of the soul with God the Father.

Doctor and patroness

She died in Rome on April 29, 1380, only thirty-three years old. She was canonized in 1461, proclaimed patroness of Italy together with Saint Francis, and a Doctor of the Church in 1970 by Paul VI. In 1999 John Paul II declared her co-patroness of Europe. She used to say: "If you are what you should be, you will set the whole world on fire."
jeronimo:
A student in love with books

Jerome was born around 347 in Stridon, in Dalmatia, near today's border between Croatia and Slovenia. As a young man he went to study in Rome, where he learned grammar, rhetoric and the Latin classics, which he loved deeply. There he was baptized. Later he traveled through Gaul and Italy and, together with friends, began to long for a life wholly devoted to God.

The hermit of the desert

He set out for the East and lived for some years as a hermit in the desert of Chalcis, in Syria, amid fasting, work and study. He himself tells that during an illness he dreamed he was standing before God's judgment seat and heard: "You are a Ciceronian, not a Christian," because he preferred pagan books to the Scriptures. From then on he decided to devote his intelligence to the Word of God. There he began learning Hebrew from a converted Jew, a task he himself found extremely hard. He was ordained a priest in Antioch and also studied in Constantinople.

The Vulgate

In 382 he returned to Rome and became secretary to Pope Damasus, who asked him to revise the Latin translation of the Gospels. He also guided a group of Roman noblewomen who wanted to study the Bible and live simply, such as Saint Paula and Saint Marcella. After Damasus died he left Rome and went to live in Bethlehem, near the grotto of Jesus' birth, where he founded monasteries with Paula. There, for more than thirty years, he translated almost the entire Bible directly from Hebrew and Greek into Latin. This translation, called the Vulgate, was used by the Western Church for more than a thousand years.

"Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ"

Jerome had a fiery temper and wrote harsh letters against those he thought were wrong, but he knew how to recognize his faults and wept over them. He died in Bethlehem on September 30, 420. He is a Doctor of the Church and patron of translators, librarians and students of the Bible. Because of him, September is dedicated to the Bible in many countries. Art usually shows him with a lion, recalling an ancient legend, and with books and a skull, signs of study and penance.
ambrosio:
A governor acclaimed as bishop

Ambrose was born around 340 in Trier, in today's Germany, the son of a high official of the Roman Empire. He studied law in Rome and had a brilliant career until he was named governor of the region whose capital was Milan. In 374 the city's bishop died, and Catholics and Arians were fighting violently over who would succeed him. Ambrose went to the cathedral to keep order and spoke to the people so calmly that, according to tradition, a child cried out: "Ambrose for bishop!" The crowd took up the cry.

From catechumen to shepherd

The problem was that Ambrose was not even baptized yet: he was a catechumen, someone preparing for Baptism. He tried to flee and refuse, but finally accepted it as God's will. Within a few days he was baptized, ordained and consecrated bishop, on December 7, 374. He gave his possessions to the poor and to the Church and began studying the Scriptures and the Greek Fathers in depth, learning while he taught. He became an admirable preacher, and it was precisely his sermons that moved the young Augustine, whom he baptized at Easter 387.

Firm before emperors

Ambrose defended the freedom of the Church before the powers of the world. When Empress Justina demanded a basilica in Milan for the Arians, he refused and stayed inside the church with the people, who spent the days singing psalms and hymns in alternating choirs, a custom he introduced in the West. Later, after Emperor Theodosius ordered the massacre of thousands of people in Thessalonica, Ambrose required him to do public penance before receiving Communion again. And the emperor obeyed.

Father of the Church

He wrote treatises on the sacraments, on virginity and on the duties of the clergy, as well as beautiful hymns still sung today in the Liturgy of the Hours. He died on April 4, 397, a Holy Saturday. He is one of the four great Doctors of the Western Church and patron of Milan, and his feast is celebrated on December 7, the day of his episcopal ordination.
joao-crisostomo:
The son of a widowed mother

John was born around 349 in Antioch, one of the greatest cities of the East. His father died when he was a baby, and his mother, Anthusa, widowed at twenty, decided not to remarry so that she could raise him in the faith. He studied rhetoric under Libanius, the most famous teacher of the time, who reportedly said John would have been his successor "if the Christians had not stolen him." Baptized as a young man, he wanted to live as a monk and spent some years in penance in the mountains near Antioch, until poor health forced him to return.

The "Golden Mouth"

Ordained a priest in 386, he preached for twelve years in Antioch. His homilies explained the Bible in a simple and practical way and spoke about family life, the use of money, the Eucharist and care for the poor. People packed the churches and sometimes applauded in the middle of a sermon. That is why he later received the nickname "Chrysostom," which in Greek means "golden mouth." He said that whoever does not recognize Christ in the poor does not truly recognize him on the altar.

Archbishop of Constantinople

In 397 he was chosen, almost by force, as archbishop of Constantinople, the capital of the Empire. There he reformed the clergy, sold luxury items from the bishop's palace to support hospitals and fearlessly denounced the excesses of the rich and of the court. His words displeased Empress Eudoxia and some rival bishops, who deposed him at an unjust synod and sent him into exile. The people rose up and he was even allowed to return, but he was exiled again, first to Armenia and then to an even more distant place.

"Glory to God for all things"

Sick and forced to walk under sun and rain, he died on the road to exile, at Comana, on September 14, 407. His last words were: "Glory to God for all things." Years later his remains were brought back with honor to Constantinople. He is a Doctor of the Church and patron of preachers, and the liturgy that bears his name is still celebrated today by the Eastern Churches. His feast is September 13.
gregorio-magno:
Prefect of Rome turned monk

Gregory was born around 540 in Rome into a noble Christian family; his mother, Silvia, is also venerated as a saint. As a young man he held the office of prefect of Rome, the highest in the city. After his father's death, however, he turned the family house on the Caelian Hill into a monastery dedicated to Saint Andrew, founded six more monasteries in Sicily with his wealth and became a monk. He said those were the happiest years of his life.

Pope in a time of plague

The Pope called him back to the service of the Church: he became a deacon and spent years in Constantinople as papal representative to the emperor. In 590, when Pope Pelagius II died during a terrible plague, the clergy and people chose Gregory. He tried to refuse but finally accepted. He organized processions of penance through the city, and tradition says he saw an angel sheathing his sword above Hadrian's mausoleum, a sign that the epidemic was ending.

As pope he faced famine, floods and the threat of the Lombards. He organized the distribution of grain to the poor, negotiated peace, ransomed prisoners and wisely administered the goods of the Church. He chose for himself the title "servant of the servants of God," which popes still use today.

Missionary to England

In 596 he sent the monk Augustine and about forty companions to evangelize the Anglo-Saxons of England, which gave rise to the Church of Canterbury. He wrote the "Pastoral Rule," a handbook for bishops and priests, the "Dialogues," which tell the life of Saint Benedict, and biblical commentaries such as his great work on Job. He took care of the liturgy, and for that reason the chant of the Church of Rome became known as Gregorian chant.

The Great

Though ill for much of his pontificate, he worked to the end. He died on March 12, 604. He is one of the four great Doctors of the Western Church and was called "Magnus," the Great. His feast is September 3, the day of his ordination as pope, and he is the patron of musicians, singers and teachers.
boaventura:
A "good fortune"

His baptismal name was Giovanni di Fidanza, and he was born around 1217 in Bagnoregio, near Viterbo, in Italy. As a child he became gravely ill and, as he himself recounted, was healed through the intercession of Saint Francis of Assisi. A later tradition says the name Bonaventure came from a joyful exclamation: "O, buona ventura!" ("O, good fortune!"). Grateful, he used to say he had received his very life from Francis.

Student and master in Paris

He went to study at the University of Paris and around 1243 joined the Friars Minor, the Franciscans. His teacher was the great theologian Alexander of Hales, and he soon became a professor himself. In 1257 he was recognized as a master of the university in the same period as Saint Thomas Aquinas, who was his friend. The two of them, one a Franciscan and the other a Dominican, together defended the new mendicant orders, which some professors of the time criticized.

The second founder of the Franciscans

Also in 1257, at about forty years of age, he was elected minister general of the Franciscan Order, a post he held for seventeen years. The order was growing quickly and living through tensions between those who wanted radical poverty and those who asked for adaptations. Bonaventure led the friars with balance and firmness and wrote their constitutions and the official biography of Saint Francis, the "Major Legend." That is why he is called the second founder of the order. On Mount La Verna, where Francis received the stigmata, he wrote "The Journey of the Mind into God," a path of prayer that rises from creatures to the Creator.

The Seraphic Doctor

In 1273 Pope Gregory X named him a cardinal. It is said that the envoys found him washing dishes in the friary and that he asked them to hang the cardinal's hat on a tree until he finished the job. He worked on preparing the Second Council of Lyon, which sought union with the Christians of the East, and died during the council on July 15, 1274. He was canonized in 1482 and declared a Doctor of the Church, the "Seraphic Doctor," for the burning love of his theology.
alberto-magno:
A young man curious about everything

Albert was born around 1200 in Lauingen, in Bavaria, into a family of knights. He went to study in Padua, in Italy, where he fell in love with nature and philosophy. There he met the Dominicans and, moved by the preaching of Jordan of Saxony, Saint Dominic's successor, he joined the order around 1223, despite his family's opposition.

Teacher of Thomas Aquinas

He taught in several friaries in Germany and later at the University of Paris, where he became a master of theology. Among his students was a quiet, large young man, Thomas Aquinas, whom his classmates called the "dumb ox." Albert recognized his genius and took him to Cologne, where in 1248 he founded a Dominican house of studies. Later, after Thomas's death, Albert traveled to Paris in his old age to defend his former student's ideas.

Scientist, friar and bishop

Albert wrote about almost everything studied in his day: philosophy, theology, logic, astronomy, plants, animals, minerals and geography. He commented on the works of Aristotle and made direct observations of nature, something rare at the time. That is why he received the title "Universal Doctor." For him, studying creation was a way of praising the Creator, and faith and science were not enemies.

He was elected superior of the Dominicans of Germany and visited the friaries traveling on foot, as the rule required. In 1260 the Pope named him bishop of Regensburg, where he put the diocese in order, but after two years he asked to resign and return to teaching and preaching. He spent his last years in Cologne, praying and studying.

Patron of scientists

He died in Cologne on November 15, 1280. He was canonized and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931 by Pope Pius XI, and ten years later Pius XII proclaimed him patron of those who devote themselves to the natural sciences. He is remembered as an example that intelligence and faith can walk together, with humility before the mystery of God.
joao-da-cruz:
A childhood of poverty

Juan de Yepes was born in 1542 in Fontiveros, near Ávila, in Spain. His father died when he was small, and his mother, Catalina, raised her children in such deep poverty that one of his brothers died of hunger. The family moved to Medina del Campo, where John worked in a hospital caring for the sick and studied with the Jesuits. In 1563 he joined the Carmelites and went to study at the University of Salamanca.

The meeting with Teresa

Longing for a life of greater silence and prayer, he was thinking of becoming a Carthusian. In 1567, however, he met Saint Teresa of Ávila, who was looking for friars to bring the reform of Carmel to the men as well. Teresa convinced him, and the following year, in a poor little house in Duruelo, he began with others the first community of Discalced Carmelite friars, taking the name John of the Cross. He later became confessor to the nuns of the Monastery of the Incarnation in Ávila, where Teresa was prioress.

The prison in Toledo

The reform provoked strong opposition within the order itself. In December 1577, friars opposed to it kidnapped John and locked him up in the friary of Toledo, in a tiny, dark cell with almost no light. For about nine months he was humiliated and flogged, but it was there, in the darkness, that he composed from memory some of the most beautiful verses in the Spanish language, such as those of the "Spiritual Canticle." In August 1578 he managed to escape at night, climbing down a rope made from strips of blanket.

The Mystical Doctor

Once free, he served as superior of several houses and guided many souls. He wrote "The Ascent of Mount Carmel," "The Dark Night," "The Spiritual Canticle" and "The Living Flame of Love," in which he describes the soul's path, through purification, to union with God. At the end of his life he was removed from office, fell ill and suffered misunderstanding, but he accepted everything in peace. He died in Úbeda on the night of December 14, 1591, saying he was going to sing Matins in heaven. He was canonized in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926. His are the words: "In the evening of life we will be judged on love."
hildegarda:
The girl of the "living light"

Hildegard was born in 1098 in Bermersheim, in the Rhine region of Germany, the tenth child of a noble family. From the age of three she said she saw a light she called "the shadow of the living light," but she kept it to herself. At eight she was entrusted to Jutta of Sponheim, a young woman who lived in enclosure beside the Benedictine monastery of Disibodenberg. There she learned to pray the psalms, to read Latin and to love monastic life, and later she made her vows as a nun.

"Write what you see"

When Jutta died in 1136, the nuns chose Hildegard as their superior. At forty-two she received in a vision the command to write down what she saw and heard. Afraid, she hesitated, but with the support of a monk and of her confessor she began writing "Scivias" ("Know the Ways"). Saint Bernard of Clairvaux encouraged her, and Pope Eugene III, at a synod in Trier, read parts of the work and approved her continuing to write. From then on her fame spread throughout Europe.

Abbess, composer and preacher

Around 1150 she founded a new monastery on the Rupertsberg near Bingen, and later another at Eibingen. She wrote letters to popes, bishops, emperors such as Frederick Barbarossa and to ordinary people, giving advice and sometimes boldly rebuking them. In old age she made preaching journeys to several cities, something extremely rare for a woman of her time. She composed dozens of liturgical chants and a musical drama, the "Ordo Virtutum," still sung and recorded today. She also wrote books on plants, animals, stones and the health of the human body.

Doctor of the Church

She died on September 17, 1179, in her monastery on the Rupertsberg. She was venerated as a saint for centuries, especially in Germany, and in 2012 Pope Benedict XVI extended her cult to the whole Church and proclaimed her a Doctor of the Church, the fourth woman to receive that title. She is remembered as a woman who united faith, intelligence, art and care for creation, always in the service of God.
afonso-ligorio:
The lawyer who lost a case

Alphonsus Maria de Liguori was born on September 27, 1696, near Naples, Italy, into a noble family. Highly gifted, he earned a doctorate in law at sixteen and became one of the most brilliant lawyers in the city, said to have gone years without losing a case. In 1723, however, he lost a very important lawsuit because he had overlooked a detail in a document. Humiliated, he understood that the world and success were passing things and decided to change his life.

"Leave the world and give yourself to me"

Soon afterward, while visiting the sick in a Naples hospital, he felt the call in his heart: "Leave the world and give yourself to me." He went to a church of Our Lady of Mercy and laid his nobleman's sword before the altar as a sign of surrender. Against his father's wishes he studied theology and was ordained a priest in 1726. He devoted himself to the poorest: he preached in the outskirts of Naples and organized evening prayer groups for laborers, fishermen and ordinary people.

Founder of the Redemptorists

When he saw the spiritual misery of the abandoned peasants in the mountains, he founded in 1732 the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, the Redemptorists, to bring popular missions to the most forgotten places. He wrote more than a hundred works: "Moral Theology," which helped confessors unite truth with mercy, "The Glories of Mary," "Visits to the Blessed Sacrament" and even the Italian Christmas carol "Tu scendi dalle stelle." In 1762 he was named bishop of Sant'Agata dei Goti, where he worked tirelessly despite fragile health.

An old age marked by the cross

In his last years he suffered from arthritis that bent his neck so badly that his chin touched his chest. Because of intrigues he was even cut off from the congregation he had founded, but he accepted everything with humility. He died on August 1, 1787, almost ninety-one years old. He was canonized in 1839, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1871 and is the patron of confessors and moral theologians.
joao-henry-newman:
A young Anglican at Oxford

John Henry Newman was born in London on February 21, 1801, into an Anglican family. At fifteen he went through a powerful inner conversion and decided to give his life to God. He studied at the University of Oxford, became a fellow and, in 1828, vicar of the university church of Saint Mary's, where his sermons drew students and professors alike. On a sea voyage in the Mediterranean, ill and far from home, he wrote the famous hymn "Lead, Kindly Light."

The Oxford Movement

From 1833 he led, with friends, the so-called Oxford Movement, which sought to rediscover the ancient roots of the faith in the Church of England. As he studied the Fathers of the Church from the first centuries, Newman gradually realized that the Church that had faithfully preserved that heritage was the Catholic Church. The conclusion cost him years of prayer and suffering, because it meant leaving friends, prestige and a brilliant career. He withdrew to a life of prayer at Littlemore and, on October 9, 1845, was received into the Catholic Church by the Passionist priest Dominic Barberi.

Priest, educator and cardinal

Ordained a priest in Rome in 1847, he founded the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri in Birmingham, England, where he lived the rest of his life serving the poor and caring for souls. He was rector of the new Catholic University of Ireland in Dublin and wrote "The Idea of a University," on the complete formation of the person. Accused of being insincere in his conversion, he answered with the "Apologia pro Vita Sua," the story of his soul, which moved England. In 1879 Pope Leo XIII made him a cardinal, and he chose as his motto "heart speaks to heart."

Saint and Doctor of the Church

He died in Birmingham on August 11, 1890. He was beatified by Benedict XVI in 2010 and canonized by Pope Francis in 2019. In 2025 Pope Leo XIV proclaimed him a Doctor of the Church and co-patron of education, together with Saint Thomas Aquinas. He taught that conscience is the voice of God in the heart and that sincerely seeking the truth leads to Christ. His feast is October 9.
joao-paulo-ii:
Karol of Wadowice

Karol Józef Wojtyła was born on May 18, 1920, in Wadowice, Poland. As a boy he lost his mother; years later his older brother, a doctor, died, and then his father, with whom he prayed every night. A young man of many gifts, he loved sports, poetry and theater, and went to study literature at the University of Kraków. During the Nazi occupation he worked in a quarry and a chemical factory while taking part in an underground theater that kept Polish culture alive.

Priest, bishop and cardinal

In 1942 he entered an underground seminary and was ordained a priest on November 1, 1946. He studied in Rome, became a university professor and a priest very close to young people, going on hikes, camping trips and kayaking excursions with them while talking about faith, love and family. At thirty-eight he was named auxiliary bishop of Kraków, then archbishop and cardinal, and he took part in the Second Vatican Council.

"Do not be afraid!"

On October 16, 1978, he was elected Pope, the first non-Italian in more than 450 years. He began his pontificate saying: "Do not be afraid! Open wide the doors to Christ!" His first visit to Poland, in 1979, gave courage to a people under communist rule. On May 13, 1981, he was shot in Saint Peter's Square; he survived, attributed his life to Our Lady of Fatima and went to prison to forgive the man who had shot him.

He made more than a hundred journeys around the world, including to Brazil, created World Youth Day, published the Catechism of the Catholic Church, added the Luminous Mysteries to the Rosary and instituted Divine Mercy Sunday when he canonized Saint Faustina. He defended the dignity of every human life, from conception to natural death.

Saint of the Church

In his last years, living with Parkinson's disease, he taught the value of suffering lived with faith. He died on April 2, 2005, the eve of Divine Mercy Sunday, and the crowd in Rome shouted "Santo subito!" ("A saint at once!"). He was beatified in 2011 and canonized in 2014. His feast is October 22, the day his pontificate began.
francisco-assis:
The rich merchant's son

Francis was born in Assisi, Italy, around 1182, the son of Pietro Bernardone, a wealthy cloth merchant, and his wife Pica. A cheerful, generous young man who led the city's parties, he dreamed of becoming a knight. He fought in the war between Assisi and Perugia, spent about a year as a prisoner and came home ill. Soon afterward, on his way to another battle, he heard a question in a dream: is it better to serve the lord or the servant? He went back home and began searching for what God wanted of him.

"Go and repair my house"

One day, overcoming the disgust he felt, he got down from his horse and embraced a leper. Later, praying before the crucifix in the little church of San Damiano, he heard: "Francis, go and repair my house, which is falling into ruin." To restore the church he sold some of his father's cloth, and his father, furious, took him before the bishop. There Francis gave everything back, even his clothes, saying: "From now on I will say only: Our Father who art in heaven." He began to live in poverty, rebuilding chapels and caring for lepers.

The lesser brothers

When he heard the Gospel in which Jesus sends out the disciples without gold or a bag, he understood his vocation. Soon other young men joined him, and in 1209 Pope Innocent III approved their way of life. The Friars Minor were born. In 1212 Saint Clare also left everything, beginning the Poor Clares. Francis preached peace, conversion and love for all creation, calling the sun, the moon, water and even death his brothers and sisters. In 1219 he went to Egypt and spoke peacefully with the sultan. At Christmas 1223, in Greccio, he set up the first living nativity scene.

The stigmata and Brother Sun

In 1224, on Mount La Verna, he received in his body the wounds of the crucified Christ. Almost blind and very ill, he composed the "Canticle of the Creatures." He died at the Portiuncula, lying on the bare ground, on the night of October 3, 1226. He was canonized only two years later. He is patron of Italy and of ecology, and his feast is October 4.
jose:
The descendant of David

Saint Joseph appears in the Gospels as a descendant of King David and a carpenter in Nazareth, a small village in Galilee. He was betrothed to Mary when he learned that she was expecting a child. The Gospel of Matthew calls him a "just man": not wanting to expose her, he planned to send her away quietly. Then an angel appeared to him in a dream and explained that the child was from the Holy Spirit, asking him to take Mary into his home and give the boy the name Jesus. Joseph woke up and did exactly as the angel had commanded.

Guardian of the Holy Family

Because of a census, he took Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born. Three more times God spoke to Joseph in a dream, and he always obeyed promptly: he fled by night to Egypt when Herod wanted to kill the Child, came back when the danger had passed and went to live in Nazareth. There he taught Jesus his trade, so that people called Jesus "the carpenter's son." The Gospels record not a single word spoken by Joseph; he is the saint of silence, of listening and of action.

The last time he appears is when, with Mary, he searches for twelve-year-old Jesus, who had stayed behind in the Temple in Jerusalem. Tradition holds that Joseph died before Jesus began his public life, in the arms of Jesus and Mary. That is why he is invoked as the patron of a happy death.

Patron of the Church

Devotion to Saint Joseph grew greatly over the centuries. Saint Teresa of Ávila said she never asked him for anything without being heard. In 1870 Pope Pius IX proclaimed him Patron of the Universal Church. Pius XII created the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker on May 1, and John XXIII placed his name in the Eucharistic Prayer. In 2020 Pope Francis published the letter "With a Father's Heart" and dedicated an entire year to him.

A model of fatherhood

Saint Joseph is the patron of fathers, families, workers and those looking for a home. He is a model of faith that trusts even without understanding everything, of honest work and of love that protects without seeking attention. His solemnity is celebrated on March 19.
padre-pio:
Francesco of Pietrelcina

Francesco Forgione was born on May 25, 1887, in Pietrelcina, a poor village in southern Italy, into a deeply religious peasant family. From childhood he prayed a great deal and said he talked with his guardian angel. To pay for his studies, his father even emigrated to work in the United States. At fifteen he joined the Capuchin friars, receiving the name Pio, and despite fragile health he was ordained a priest on August 10, 1910.

The stigmata

In 1916 he was sent to the friary of San Giovanni Rotondo, on the Gargano peninsula, where he lived the rest of his life. On September 20, 1918, while praying before a crucifix, the wounds of Christ appeared on his hands, feet and side, and he bore them painfully for fifty years, hiding his hands in gloves. The news drew crowds and also suspicion: the Church investigated carefully and for some years he was forbidden to celebrate Mass in public and to receive the people. Padre Pio obeyed in silence, saying obedience was his greatest treasure.

The confessor and the Mass

His Mass could last for hours, celebrated with deep recollection, as one living Calvary. He spent many hours a day in the confessional, and many said he read hearts and called sinners to conversion with firmness and tenderness. Many people reported graces, healings and other extraordinary gifts attributed to him. He founded Prayer Groups and in 1956 opened a large hospital, the "Home for the Relief of Suffering," to care for the sick with skill and love.

"Pray, hope and don't worry"

He died on September 23, 1968, shortly after the wounds had disappeared from his body. More than a hundred thousand people came to his funeral. Pope John Paul II, who as a young priest had gone to confession to him, beatified him in 1999 and canonized him in 2002. He is one of the most beloved saints of our time, and his advice is still timely: "Pray, hope and don't worry."
faustina:
Helena, the peasant girl

Helena Kowalska was born on August 25, 1905, in Głogowiec, Poland, the third of ten children of a poor peasant family. She had less than three years of schooling. From the age of seven she felt in her heart a call to religious life, but her parents could not help her. At sixteen she went to work as a housemaid to support her family.

"How long shall I put up with you?"

One day, at a dance with her sister, she saw the suffering Jesus, who asked her how long he would have to be patient with her. Helena left, went into a church and soon afterward set out for Warsaw with nothing but the clothes she was wearing, determined to enter a convent. After several refusals she was accepted in 1925 by the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy, where she received the name Sister Maria Faustina of the Most Blessed Sacrament. In the convent she worked as a cook, gardener and portress, always in simple tasks.

"Jesus, I trust in you"

On February 22, 1931, in Płock, Jesus appeared to her dressed in white, with two rays coming from his heart, one red and one pale, and asked that an image be painted with the words "Jesus, I trust in you." He also asked for a feast of Mercy on the Sunday after Easter. With the help of her confessor, Father Michael Sopoćko, the first image was painted in 1934 in Vilnius. At his direction Faustina kept a diary recording Jesus' messages about God's mercy toward sinners. In it are the Chaplet of Divine Mercy and the request to remember the Passion at three in the afternoon, the Hour of Mercy.

Apostle of Mercy

Suffering from tuberculosis, she offered her pain for the salvation of souls. She died in Kraków on October 5, 1938, only thirty-three years old. Pope John Paul II canonized her on April 30, 2000, and on that same day instituted Divine Mercy Sunday for the whole Church. Her feast is October 5.
dulce-pobres:
The girl who opened the door to the poor

Maria Rita de Souza Brito Lopes Pontes was born in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, on May 26, 1914. She lost her mother at six. While still a teenager she began welcoming beggars and sick people at her front door, which her family jokingly called "Saint Francis's gatehouse." In 1933 she joined the Congregation of the Missionary Sisters of the Immaculate Conception of the Mother of God and received the name Sister Dulce, in honor of her mother.

From a chicken coop to a hospital

Back in Salvador, Sister Dulce devoted herself to workers, the poor and the sick who lived on the streets and in stilt houses. In 1936 she founded the Saint Francis Workers' Union, one of the first Christian workers' movements in Bahia. To shelter the sick she even occupied empty houses, from which she was evicted, until she took them to the arches of a church. In 1949, with her superior's permission, she turned the convent's chicken coop into a shelter for seventy sick people. From that chicken coop grew the Santo Antônio Hospital, which became one of the largest free health care complexes in Brazil, the Sister Dulce Social Works.

The strength of a frail woman

Small and of fragile health, she lived for decades with greatly reduced lung capacity, sleeping little, often sitting in a chair. She asked for help from businessmen, politicians and anyone she met, always in the name of the poor. It is said that a merchant spat in her hand when she asked for a donation, and she calmly replied: "That was for me; now give something for my poor." In 1988 she was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize. Pope John Paul II met her twice, the last time on her deathbed in 1991.

The Good Angel of Bahia

She died on March 13, 1992, in Salvador, mourned by the whole country. She was beatified in 2011 and canonized by Pope Francis on October 13, 2019, becoming the first woman saint born in Brazil. Her feast is August 13. She used to say: "Love overcomes every obstacle, every sacrifice."
teresa-calcuta:
Gonxha of Skopje

Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu was born on August 26, 1910, in Skopje, today the capital of North Macedonia, into a Catholic Albanian family. Her father died when she was eight, and her mother raised the children with faith and generosity, always opening their home to the poor. At eighteen, feeling called to the missions, she joined the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland and was soon sent to India. She chose the name Teresa in honor of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux.

The call within a call

For almost twenty years she was a teacher and later principal at a girls' school in Calcutta. On September 10, 1946, on a train journey, she felt what she called a "call within a call": to leave the convent and serve Jesus in the poorest of the poor, hearing from him the words "I thirst." With the Church's permission, in 1948 she exchanged her habit for a simple white sari with blue borders, took a nursing course and began, all alone, an open-air school in a slum.

The Missionaries of Charity

Soon some of her former students joined her, and in 1950 the Congregation of the Missionaries of Charity was born. In 1952 she opened a home for the dying abandoned on the streets, so they could die with dignity, surrounded by love. Then came orphanages, centers for lepers and houses all over the world, including in Brazil. In 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize and asked that the money for the banquet be given to the poor. Letters published after her death revealed that for many years she lived through a deep interior darkness, without feeling God's presence, yet she kept loving and serving faithfully and with a smile.

Saint of the poor

She died in Calcutta on September 5, 1997. She was beatified in 2003 and canonized by Pope Francis on September 4, 2016. She used to say that we are not called to do great things, but small things with great love. Her feast is September 5.
bernadete:
The miller's daughter

Bernadette Soubirous was born on January 7, 1844, in Lourdes, in southern France, the daughter of a miller who fell into poverty. The family even lived in a damp, dark former jail cell called "le cachot." Bernadette had asthma, could barely read and at fourteen was still preparing for her First Communion, because she had trouble learning the catechism.

The Lady of the grotto

On February 11, 1858, while gathering firewood near the grotto of Massabielle beside the river, Bernadette saw a young lady dressed in white, with a blue sash, a rosary in her hands and golden roses on her feet. Until July of that year the Lady appeared eighteen times. She asked for prayer and penance for the conversion of sinners, for processions to be held and for a chapel to be built there. One day she pointed to a spot on the ground and asked Bernadette to drink from the spring: she dug with her hands, and there flowed the spring that still runs today. On March 25, when asked her name, the Lady answered in the local dialect: "I am the Immaculate Conception," words Bernadette did not even understand, but which the Pope had proclaimed as dogma four years earlier.

Questioned, but firm

Bernadette was questioned many times by the police, the parish priest and the authorities, and she never changed her story or sought any advantage. In 1862 the bishop recognized the apparitions. To escape curiosity, in 1866 she entered the Sisters of Charity of Nevers, where she lived hidden, humble and very ill. She said Our Lady had used her like a broom: after it is used, the broom goes back behind the door.

Saint of Lourdes

She died on April 16, 1879, at thirty-five. Her body, found preserved years later, rests in Nevers. She was canonized in 1933. Lourdes became one of the greatest shrines in the world, where millions of pilgrims and sick people pray every year. Her feast is April 16.
joana-darc:
The peasant girl of Domrémy

Joan of Arc was born around 1412 in Domrémy, a village in eastern France, into a peasant family. France was living through the Hundred Years' War against England, with much of the country occupied. Joan tended the animals, spun wool and prayed a great deal. At thirteen she began to hear voices she identified as those of Saint Michael the Archangel, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret, calling her to a mission: to help the heir to the throne, Charles, set France free.

From Chinon to Orléans

In 1429, at about seventeen, she managed to be brought to the Dauphin Charles at Chinon. After being examined by theologians, she received armor and a banner bearing the names of Jesus and Mary. She required the soldiers to go to confession, stop blaspheming and attend Mass. In May 1429, leading the troops, she freed the city of Orléans, which had been besieged for months, and won other victories. On July 17, with her at his side, Charles was crowned king in the cathedral of Reims.

Capture and trial

In 1430 Joan was captured at Compiègne by the Burgundians and sold to the English. She was tried in Rouen by a church court manipulated by political interests. Though she had no education, she answered with a wisdom that astonished the judges. When they tried to trap her by asking whether she was in God's grace, she replied: "If I am not, may God put me there; if I am, may God keep me there." She was unjustly condemned and, on May 30, 1431, at nineteen years of age, she was burned at the stake in the market square of Rouen, holding a cross and calling on the name of Jesus.

Declared innocent

In 1456 a new trial, requested by her mother and authorized by the Pope, declared that the trial had been unjust and annulled the sentence. Joan was canonized in 1920 by Pope Benedict XV and is a patron saint of France. She is remembered as an example of courage, purity and faithfulness to God to the very end. Her feast is May 30.
lourenco:
Deacon of Rome

Lawrence lived in the third century and, according to an ancient tradition, came from Hispania, today's Spain. In Rome he was one of the seven deacons of Pope Sixtus II, responsible for caring for the goods of the Church and for distributing help to the poor, widows and orphans. That is why he was so well known and loved by the needy of the city.

The persecution of Valerian

In 258 Emperor Valerian ordered a harsh persecution of Christians, especially bishops, priests and deacons. On August 6 of that year, Pope Sixtus II was arrested while celebrating with the faithful in the catacombs and was executed along with some of his deacons. Tradition says that Lawrence, seeing him led to death, asked to go with him, and the Pope answered that in three days Lawrence would follow him in an even greater struggle.

"These are the treasures of the Church"

The prefect of Rome, believing the Church kept great riches, demanded that Lawrence hand them over. The deacon asked for a few days to gather them. During that time he distributed everything the community owned to the poor. Then he came back with a crowd of poor people, sick, blind, orphans and widows and said: "These are the treasures of the Church." Furious, the prefect condemned him to a cruel death.

According to the tradition handed down by Saint Ambrose and other ancient writers, Lawrence was slowly roasted on a gridiron and, even in the midst of his suffering, kept such peace that he said to his executioners: "Turn me over, this side is done." He died on August 10, 258, praying for the conversion of Rome.

One of the best-loved martyrs

Over his tomb the basilica of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls was built in Rome, and his name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass. He is the patron of deacons, of the poor and of cooks. In several countries the shooting stars of mid-August are popularly called "the tears of Saint Lawrence." His feast is August 10.
